Tesla and SpaceX also employ thousands of immigrant engineers, including many on H-1B visas from India and China.

And here’s a simple test: actually listen to Musk’s full interviews instead of reading headlines about them. Whether you agree with him or not, you’ll often find his position is more nuanced than the media portrays. Take the current debate over “remigration.” What he’s consistently emphasized is removing people who are in the country illegally or who commit serious crimes. You can support or oppose that policy, but calling it “racist” skips over the actual argument.

By all means criticize Musk where the facts support it. But judge him by the totality of his actions, his hiring record, and what he actually says in context, not by selectively quoted headlines.

Balance—not extremes—is where health thrives. As many commenters have pointed out, our healthcare system often focuses more on treating disease than promoting health. Many of the pillars of lifestyle medicine—nutrition, exercise, sleep, stress management, and metabolic health—receive far too little attention during routine care.

Wearable technology can help fill that gap, but only if you're curious and willing to act on the information. If tracking data creates anxiety, a wearable may not be the right tool. But for many people, short-term use of a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) can be eye-opening. I encourage my cancer patients to wear one for 2–4 weeks to discover how simple changes—such as eating vegetables before carbohydrates, taking a walk after meals, or increasing resistant starches—can improve their metabolic health.

Devices like the Oura Ring or WHOOP can also provide valuable insights into sleep, recovery, and heart rate variability (HRV), a useful marker of nervous system resilience. The value comes from observing trends over months, not reacting to a single week's worth of data.

As an integrative cancer care physician, I think of wearables not as gadgets, but as tools that empower patients to better understand their bodies and cultivate a healthier internal terrain.

I also do use home cortisol testing - not as the company recommends - but as snap shots about my training load. The data has been helpful for me to track and improve my training and has helped me listen to my body - if the numbers are different than how I feel I am pretty good about taking it in stride and just going by how I feel but overall I have gotten good information. 
Having said that, I am NOT a fan of imaging for screening - even with breast cancer, screening did NOT change mortality - just made us overtreat early cancers. It was the improved chemo that changed mortality - new classes of drugs. 
No way would I ever recommend full body imaging. And it would have likely caught my brain tumor earlier but may not have changed treatment - likely it would have been followed until I became symptomatic (which is when we found it).

What seems like a simple “soak the rich” idea has much complexity. NYC has a number of days test for tax domicile and one must keep meticulous records of where you were at midnight each day if you want to avoid a tax challenge (although your own records may be challenged). The common law of domicile is different. Domicile once acquired is presumed to continue based on intent and continuation of contacts with your history of domicile. The application of these standards is often abused by the courts where the standard of proof for leaving a high-tax domicile is often higher than than the standard of proof for one unintentionally spending time in the high-tax domicile. 

There is a peculiar Massachusetts case in which someone had a short visit to Boston arriving by plane as they considered maybe moving to Boston. Eventually they did move so the MA could found they acquired a MA domicile as of the time the plane landed. The hook was intention after the fact and the mere nexus of landing in MA was enough. There are other cases where with very similar facts the courts reached very different conclusions. Hindsight becomes foresight. 

So, what will be the criteria for someone with two homes, one in NYC and one elsewhere. Consider if they spent 60% of their time in NYC one year, but only 40% in the next year. A court could rule either way as to the tax domicile for which is the second home. 

For the unwilling taxpayers, the solution is a five-letter word - HOTEL

This story is emblematic of a recurring pattern in American history. We ask extraordinary things of military personnel, first responders, and others who perform dangerous work, and then fail to investigate or address the long-term health consequences when they emerge. 

Shell shock (PTSD), illnesses resulting from wars, and the health effects experienced by many first responders all illustrate how our institutions have been slow to acknowledge harm, even when those affected have been raising concerns for years. 

A society that values service has an obligation not only to honor sacrifice, but also to rigorously investigate credible evidence of injury and provide appropriate care. Ignoring or delaying that responsibility undermines the very people we ask to assume the greatest risks on our behalf.

A nation that truly values service has an obligation not only to honor sacrifice, but also to rigorously investigate credible evidence of injury and provide appropriate care. 

Instead, we too often celebrate a caricature of toughness that prizes stoicism and machismo over science and endurance over accountability. It is a warrior culture that applauds strength while people are useful and then looks away once they are injured. 

Nothing captures that dysfunctional ethos more vividly than our Dear Leader celebrating the spectacle of combat by staging MMA on the White House lawn, while those who bear the lasting physical and neurological costs of service struggle to be heard.

Regarding religion and clocks - a memory from the 1960's - meeting my soon to be grandmother-in-law, for the first time mid-summer 1960's, I quietly mentioned to my fiance that her kitchen clock was an hour slow.  She heard me, and I was told that it was set to "God's Time" year round.   :-)

A Christian, she was born in 1885 and saw things go from Queen Victoria's days to Man Landing on the Moon - quite a lot of changes and didn't like anyone monkeying around with what time it was.  In her beloved memory we keep a clock set on EST year round.

These days I would like to see clocks set to DST year round. - Sorry Grandma Thomas ---

Having the Sabbath start at 530pm rather than 430pm in the winter will make life much Much MUCH easier for Sabbath-observamt Jews and for Jews who would like to observe the Sabbath but can't leave their jobs early. Observing the Sabbath is much Much MUCH more important than attending morning services in synagogue.

comments.name: Nancy P
comments.body: I have bad, cold memories of going to the school bus stop in the dark in winter as a child in the 1970s.  And I was lucky that I didn't have to walk to school or cross any busy streets, and that my neighborhood had sidewalks.  I also lived in Virginia, so it wasn't that cold, compared to where I live now, where it can be extremely cold and icy in winter.  And that neighborhood was generally safer than the one I live in now.  I would not want my own child walking to school in the dark at any age. Children and youth already have a hard time getting up that early and will suffer yet more sleep deprivation.  I'd prefer the status quo or year-around standard time.

comments.name: Karen
comments.body: Just to add my two cents I am an early riser (I clock in to work at 6 AM) who is in favor of permanent daylight savings time. I like more daylight hours when I'm off work, not when I'm at work. I remember as a kid in NYC the winter we had daylight savings time in effect and I was out walking to the bus before dawn in the dark for at the most two weeks.  It felt special and the one morning it started to snow was an incredibly magical experience which I have never forgotten. I still treasure the memory of that morning. I also don't remember anybody dying but NYC kids are raised to be street smart even before dawn.

comments.body:
LW1 is not describing someone who needs help. They are describing someone who is spiraling out of control. Establish a firm move-out date. One that is far enough away they can get themselves together and get a job, and close enough for your peace. They may have been a degreed elite at one point, but with a felony conviction for what sounds like a sex crime, their new station in life is low end service work. They clearly don't like that, but it's their bed, they made it, and they need to sleep in it.

Your partner needs to be clear the assistance ends at that point beyond the normal family emotional support. We had to do this with my sibling who was in a debt spiral. She still interacts with us normally, but when she calls and says she needs money for something, we all politely end the conversation and give her some space to work out how to clean up her own finances. I'm the trustee for the family trust and I've told her she's getting the disbursement on schedule and that's it.

Sometimes people need to be allowed to hit rock bottom to pick themselves up. Sometimes people find their way into the Marianas Trench. Nothing you, or your partner, can do about it if they're going diving.

The top security official in the US, the just confirmed DNI director, has no experience in the intelligence field as required by law.
﻿
His qualification for Trump is that he wants to downsize the agency to near nothingness.  The agency was set up by recommendation of the 9/11 commission to cure the silo-mentality, in-fighting that was pervasive in US intelligence groups before 9/11, e.g. CIA, FBI, military intelligence, ...

On the tactical side, there is a growing munitions shortage for the US military.  Estimates are that the US had 2300 Patriot missiles before the war. It is now down to about 800.

The current estimate is that Iran has 1000 to 1500 intermediate range ballistic missiles still available.

The defense protocol is to fire 2 Patriot missiles at an incoming missile, in order to improve the odds on intercepting the missile, i.e. a 90% success rate for one Patriot goes to a 99% success rate for two.

So it looks like the US will run out of Patriots before Iran runs out of missiles. Using multi-million dollar Patriots to fire at $50,000 drone swarms would be insane.

Iran may have decided, rightly or wrongly, that it now holds better cards.

comments.name: Roberto Foxalinni
comments.body:
As a teacher at a Liberal Arts university being whittled away thanks to the GOP's longtime disdain, one thing always frustrated me as a recruiter for my college. Searching through corporation recruiting ads. 

Corps. want people who: Know how to collaborate, can see connections, communicate well, and ask questions. 

This is exactly what a liberal arts degree does. We teach students how to think and analyze data objectively, show connections; ie how poetry can be connected to finance, how writing and literature can be connected to science, how to inform our colleagues in meaningful communications. 

Studies show students with LA degrees are more flexible than the ones with a specialty degree:  The "to a hammer every problem looks like a nail" syndrome. 

It is the questions part of things corporations don't like. Unimaginative middle managers asked why things are done in this way because its inefficient and can be done better using a new way are threatened. 

The GOP has hated higher education since Reagan got burned by the Berkely riots. The GOP relentlessly attacks higher ed  trying to bring it all down. And now with WWE exec Linda McMahan running the Dept. Of Ed, they'rey getting their wish. 

But, be careful what you wish for... 

Europe's brain drain of the US has begun, and we are already suffering from the lack of students with a Liberal Arts education.   

As a LA grad myself, I can see the connections already, unlike most others at the Dept. of Ed.

comments.body: Actually, this article is a bit misleading. The best way to see that is by considering the mission and legacy of well-regarded, Christian colleges and universities like Hillsdale College, Belmont Abbey College, Manhattan University, St. John's University, etc. A number of Christian institutions, like Hillsdale College, are often regarded as "Conservative"; the others, including Jesuit institutions like Fordham and Fairfield Universities, also believe that the "liberal arts"--e.g., philosophy, literature, theology, languages, etc.--are crucial to our shared humanity and culture; analytical thinking; and basic empathy for others. In fact, Hillsdale College is among those which advertise their emphasis on the liberal arts. It is important that the author, and others, take a fuller view of the reality of thought in our society and institutions of higher learning.

Learning, it was emphasized, was not just a four-year endeavor but a life-long activity, the benefits of which went beyond the acquisition of information to include self-knowledge and social responsibility, curiosity and critical thinking.

I'm an engineer by training.  When I was an undergrad, I dreaded my few humanities requirements as too subjective and language focused with manually typed papers (no AI!) and no spell or grammar checking, and Professors less interested in ideas and instead pedantically focused on minor language missteps.
We had a lot to learn in 4 short years and a class on Russian Lit would mean fewer math or programming classes.  Unsurprisingly, I met engineers during my career who said the classical technical curriculum itself was a waste of time "since I haven't used calculus or physics since college and would instead have wanted a class on the minutiae of heat exchanger sizing".  He had forgotten that the purpose of university was to teach you how to think and learn on your own, since you never know what you'll actually be doing in the future.
My profession is largely conservative in political outlook with an absolutist view of social problems, as if all human issues could be resolved with a bit of logic and algebra.  While the technical course demands haven't lessened over the years, our opportunities to learn outside of school have expanded.  My hope is that a few more humanities classes in the STEM curriculum might at least help us better understand the complexities of societies and if not change our political views at least get us to consider we might be wrong.

I didn't go back to teaching. Years later, I earned a degree in electrical engineering.

India’s chief justice on May 15 referred to unemployed youths as “parasites” and “cockroaches.” - this is not correct. The judge speaking in a larger context was referring to those creating unnecessary problems.

Dipke, the so called founder, has been associated with an opposition party called AAP since 2012 and was on their payroll in New Delhi government till a couple of years ago.

"On July 18, police in Delhi forcibly hospitalized a prominent environmental and educational activist"  - FALSE.  The court ordered medical care for him, so he was taken to the hospital. After a couple of days he celled of his protest and told the Dipke group to do the same.

So much potential value is lost every minute in that nation due to sweetheart deals, inspectors who only see what they've been paid to, an education system that continues to shaft the middle class, etc.

Just like we've seen here, there's only so much open corruption that people will tolerate. The Internet has made it so much harder to hide.

The "cockroaches" are the result. The main points that they want aren't particularly radical. It's poorly understood here, but the crisis started with the "exam leak crisis".

Essentially, it worked like this: students take a series of tests. Only the best students would get a shot at going to good colleges in India, or better yet, a slim shot at going to school in America or Britain. 

Well-connected kids' parents were buying the exam guides well before the test. Black marketeers were selling access. Officials were letting important people's kids see the exam before taking it.

It's not just this one thing; that's a symbol of how things have been going for Indians attempting to enter the middle class for the last 20 years. This is the landscape of my childhood: the Atlantic coast, the pine forests, the places where I still visit my parents. I was there only a few weeks ago. Watching it burn from California is heartbreaking because this is not some distant disaster. This is home going up in flames.

My family is safe today. In 2022, the fires came considerably closer. But thousands of people have now fled their homes, others have lost them entirely, and firefighters and local residents are again being asked to confront conditions that grow more dangerous each summer.

Fires are not new, and climate change does not strike every match. But extreme heat, prolonged drought and high winds increasingly determine what happens after the match is struck. Containment is therefore an enormous relief, but it is not resolution. The summer is far from over, and another heat wave is already arriving.

Five reasons limit the US to address this critical issue of cybersecurity and AI:

There has always been a tension between authoritarian government control and technological and scientific innovation. The U.S. has been the leader in both in part because of the freedom technologists and scientists have to set their own goals.  The other advantage was government funding of research. Almost every technological and scientific breakthrough since WWII started with U.S.government funding. Trump has broken the U.S. innovation machine by defunding science and by degrading scientific and technical expertise as woke. comments.body:
I find it amusing that Western 'experts' are SO concerned about the risks of AI to Beijing. 

China surges ahead, and, instead of keeping up, the US makes a sport of telling us about all the problems that Beijing will face.

In my experience, Open Source increases the safety of software. There have been so many cases where vulnerabilities have been found in Open Source code, because it is freely available for everyone to examine.

Of course it is China's goal to control the stack. Before I retired I worked on Ethernet standards for several different companies (Fujitsu, Cisco, and Huawei). Here's how it works. Your company patents its technology and then proposes that this technology becomes part of the standard. Then you trade patent rights with other companies. Cisco was the best at doing this. But, now China is doing this... and they are accused of controlling the stack. Give me a break... this is just more China-bashing.

If China wants to maintain domestic control, they will simply require that Chinese companies modify the open source accordingly. People don't have to run open source unmodified.

The idea that proprietary AI systems are safer is nonsense. I'm sure that companies developing proprietary models in the US will be forced by the US government to make specific modifications dictated by, for example, Hegseth's War Department.

Do they really think that the likes of Elon, Jeff, Alex, Peter, Mark, etc. would give two cents about what they think!

comments.name: Nogi Ichida
comments.body:
I think both the U.S. and China face many of the same risks in AI development. Some of those risks are real, while others are probably overblown. Assessing worst-case scenarios is part of what security analysts are supposed to do, but that doesn't mean those scenarios will inevitably happen.

There are risks with both open- and closed-source AI. We've seen parallels before with Linux versus Windows or macOS. As for which model ultimately proves more resilient or risky, only time will tell.

On censorship, I think many people underestimate how informed Chinese society can be. Yes, censorship has become tighter in China, but that doesn't necessarily mean people have no sense of what is happening around them. Chinese citizens are globally connected in many ways. Not criticizing the government publicly does not automatically mean they are unaware of events or differing perspectives.  AI can be very effective for propaganda purposes, but we should not underestimate our own intelligence. Technology can influence people, but it can not replace our own judgment.

To navigate censorship, many Chinese technology companies have found an equilibrium between the domestic and international markets. That is one reason companies such as TikTok and Alibaba operate different versions of their products for different markets.

By the way, a funny fact: TikTok itself is banned in China, where the domestic version, Douyin, is used instead.

comments.name: Mike
comments.body:
While it would be very disappointing to the AI community if China stops releasing models to the open source this is a case of the "horse out of the barn".   K3, GLM 5.2 and Deepseek are already out there, are extremely strong models and can do 99.99%+ of the things that people are asking AI to do.   Even if another model is never released the fact that you can get models this strong to run privately (or at a hoster) is kind of "end game".   

Going from K3 to Fable is an improvement in intelligence but you need to have questions that are hard enough to use that additional intelligence.   Very, very few questions meet that bar; there are some, but they are few and far between.   If you're working on cutting edge research, paying for the best might be worth it.   If you're doing the things most of the world wants to use AI for (communicating with their computer using natural language, writing code, generating images, working with your documents (RAG), controlling other systems (MCP)), models are basically a "solved problem" at this point, Deepseek can do it, Kimi can do it, Opus can do it; choose whatever you want, they're all capable.   

The quest for a better model has basically entered "Bugatti" territory.   Trying to build the fastest car in the world for the sake of the fastest car in the world.   Almost nobody who buys one has a hope of extracting the performance potential beyond what a Corvette would give them.  Especially when driving it in downtown NYC!

I believe China is heading into a long economic downward trend for a number of reasons.  First, demographics points to an aging population with the affects of the one child policy hampering a traditional population replacement.  That's a demand issue. 

Second, lack of social programs in Healthcare and pensions means consumers have less disposable income to spend versus savings. Again, a demand issue. 

Third, plainly the production machine China has perfected has developed produced plants now operating below capacity, coupled with trading partners lagging economies and their own demographic issues with lower birth rates.  These lead to excess inventories for producers. China can no longer count on exports as their main driver for growth -- they need to develop a strong consumer segment, and that will come with higher costs of production which will affect China's price advantages with its trading partners.

Like their massive container ships, it will take a long time to turn their economy around and I predict the middle powers/countries will have an advantage as they are already more nimble to make changes in their economies as they unwind from China's dominance.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
We are already seeing increases in wildfire intensity. At a 2.0°C rise, wildfires will intensify non-linearly due to exponential increases in Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD). Warm air holds roughly 7% more moisture per degree Celsius, aggressively drying forest canopies, soil duff, and high-elevation vegetation that once acted as natural firebreaks. Models project a doubling to quadrupling of annual burned area across Western North America and Boreal regions compared to late 20th-century baselines, along with up to a 100% increase in burned area across the Mediterranean.

This warming also expands fire seasons globally, causing Northern and Southern Hemisphere peak windows to overlap and strain firefighting resources. Higher fuel dryness triggers more frequent pyrocumulonimbus events—firestorms that generate dry lightning and spot fires miles ahead of the main front. Large high-severity burn patches will increasingly prevent natural forest recovery, risking permanent conversions to shrubland while releasing massive stores of soil carbon back into the atmosphere.

Here on the west coast of Portugal, the scorching summer of other parts of Europe, indeed other parts of Portugal,seem quite distant. Our daily temperatures have been consistently about 25-27 degrees Celsius with a constant breeze from the Atlantic. Idyllic. We have had one spate of days over 30 but that seems like a vague memory, as the forecasts call for more of the current weather for the next many days well into August. 

I say all this not to boast at my luck of having fallen upon utopic summer weather but to say how easy it is to feel like the climate crisis is not an urgent issue when, in fact it is. I say this also to shed light on how easily we can fall back into complacency after the immediate threat is over.  Indeed, I seem to have forgotten the devastating series of named storms this winter right here in the Oeste region of Portugal where I live. We endured what seemed like interminable rain and flooding. Roads were washed out. Driving, we couldn’t get to town from our village because the river crossed over the main roads. Many roads remain closed months later. We were without running water for 2 1/2 weeks as the  pipes burst and the deluge undid the water company’s repair efforts. People in some municipalities were without power for three months. Most importantly, lives and property were destroyed.  These storms were unprecedented and most assuredly because of our changing climate.

Yet, I seem to forget all that in this Western Portuguese summer.

Why make this an issue only for Jewish communities?

Making Daylight Saving Time permanent year-round is a bad idea because it would force much of the country to endure extremely late winter sunrises. Millions of people—including schoolchildren and commuters—would begin their day in darkness for weeks or months, increasing safety risks and disrupting natural sleep cycles. The extra evening daylight comes at the expense of morning light, which is more important for regulating our biological clocks. If we’re going to stop changing the clocks, permanent Standard Time—not permanent Daylight Saving Time—is the option most sleep scientists and medical organizations support.

Not that medical and scientific evidence is something that this administration relies on for anything, unfortunately.

While one does not want a situation to spiral out-of-control, it is most helpful to allow the individual time to calm themselves while administering patience and understanding. I learned this in 1976 when working solo shifts, sometimes 16 hours long, at a psychiatric half-way facility in Seattle. Resorting to physical restraints of any kind should be considered the very last option,   often counter productive to what is called for, causing fear and panic and further acting out. I have witnessed this kind of escalation on closed psychiatric wards. It is not a pretty sight.
